candidates.name: Telar
candidates.rationale: Three bold warp strands and three bold weft strands interlock in a true over/under plain weave — the exact moment separate threads resolve into one fabric, which is the whole idea of a loom orchestrating parallel autonomous runs into a single verified whole. Thin plate-colored seams between every crossing (rather than strokes or shadows) keep each thread visually distinct, so the checkerboard structure survives intact down to a 16px favicon and reads as an instantly recognizable, non-generic silhouette at 64px. The palette is just indigo plate, cream warp, and amber weft — a calm, craft-material pairing (dyed thread on indigo cloth) with strong blue/orange contrast that holds up on both light and dark Dock backgrounds without tipping into cute or corporate.

candidates.name: The Shuttle
candidates.tagline: One pass, every thread accounted for.
candidates.rationale: A single bold copper lens — the weaver's shuttle — crosses a field of narrow vertical warp threads on a deep indigo plate; the sharp taper reads instantly as "gliding tool in motion" while the perpendicular relationship (horizontal mark against vertical grid) tells the whole loom story without needing literal thread-and-needle detail. Reduced to two color families (indigo neutral + single copper accent) with a crisp dark contour on the shuttle, the silhouette survives collapse: at 64px it's unmistakably a lens crossing stripes, and at true 16px it resolves to a bright horizontal bar on a dark textured square — still distinct from a flat dot or blob, and legible on both light and dark Dock backgrounds as verified by direct rendering.

candidates.name: Telar Monogram — Woven T
candidates.rationale: At 16px the piece resolves to one unambiguous silhouette — a bold, geometric gold T on a deep indigo plate — because the crossbar and stem are solid, thick, uniform-weight strokes with no fine detail competing for pixels. At Dock scale (64–128px) a genuine over/under joint becomes visible where the stem visibly threads behind the crossbar on the left and re-emerges on top of it on the right (a real woven crossing, not a texture overlay), reinforced by a crisp seam line and sparse twill-ply strokes on each strand. Two tonal golds (lighter weft, deeper copper warp) read as one warm thread family so the shape never fragments, while the indigo-to-near-black plate gradient gives the fixed contrast needed to hold up on both light and dark Dock backgrounds. The palette (indigo + two golds) stays craft and precise — dye-and-thread, not toy yarn, not SaaS-gradient generic.

candidates.name: Direction D — The Knot
candidates.tagline: One thread, three passes, holds itself together.
candidates.rationale: A single continuous thread ties itself into a closed, self-supporting knot with exactly 3 alternating over/under crossings (each drawn as a true woven gap, not a flat overlap) — a literal picture of "the system that weaves itself" and of autonomous passes composing into one finished piece. The warm ecru-to-brass thread against a deep charcoal-indigo plate reads as craft (linen/rope on dark loom wood) rather than corporate gradient-logo or yarn-ball cute, and because the plate is fully opaque it holds identical contrast on both light and dark Docks. At 64px the three-lobed weave is clearly legible with visible over/under structure; collapsed further to a 16px favicon it still resolves to one unmistakable rounded-triangular loop silhouette in two color families (warm accent + dark neutral), satisfying the small-size legibility bar without hatching or fine detail.

scores.note: Literal plain-weave motif with correct over/under logic and fiber-matched gradients (cream warp graded top-to-bottom, gold weft graded left-to-right); reads clearly as textile from 512 down to 64px. At 16px (verified via actual-pixel raster, not just CSS-scaled vector) it degrades to a generic plaid/checkerboard grid — legible as *a* pattern but no longer distinctly 'loom,' and risks reading as a settings/table-grid utility icon. It's a repeating swatch with no single focal hierarchy, so next to sharper single-mark dock neighbors it reads as background texture rather than a logotype.

Best concept-to-brief match on paper (literal shuttle crossing warp threads, explicitly called out in the brand brief) but the weakest execution of the four. The shuttle silhouette is a plain stretched vesica/football rather than a boat-pointed shuttle, so it reads as an eye, lens, or surfboard, undercutting the metaphor it's trying to deliver. It also collapses hardest at small sizes: by 16px actual pixels it is just a flat orange bar over blue stripes with none of the shuttle concept surviving, and the little bobbin-peek triangle is illegible noise below 64px.

Strongest all-around candidate. Bold single T-monogram stays crisp and unambiguous from 512px down to 16px (confirmed on actual-pixel raster) — it never turns to mush, the rarest quality among the four. Directional warp/weft gradients and the over/under joint seam at the crossbar crossing are a genuine craft flourish that reward close inspection without cluttering the silhouette at small sizes. Reads instantly as a professional macOS app icon (bold-glyph-on-gradient-plate, in the Pages/Keynote/Notes lineage) and doubles as a wordmark tie to the product name itself.

The most technically impressive single continuous bezier at 512px — genuine premium vector craft, tasteful ivory-on-charcoal palette, holds up reasonably well at dock sizes (64-128px) where the trefoil silhouette still reads as an interlace. But there is no actual over/under weave logic (real interlacing needs visible gaps at each crossing; this is flat overlapping strokes with none), so the concept reads as a generic trinity/Celtic knot rather than a loom or fabric — closer to a wellness/jewelry mark than a build-and-verify dev tool. Collapses completely at 16px into an indistinct pale smudge with zero legible structure, the worst small-size failure of the set.

Actual plain-weave construction (true over/under interlace) — the most literal hit on 'warp/weft' and 'many strands into one fabric.' Rasterized at 16px it holds up better than expected: the blocky rects downsample into a clean, legible plaid/gingham swatch rather than mud. But it's a texture, not a mark — no focal point, so in a dock row of glyph-icons it reads as a nice fabric sample rather than a logo. Best-in-class technical polish (vignette, rim light, real interlace shadows).

At 512/64px this is the most conceptually literal 'shuttle moving across threads' — genuinely handsome, warm amber lens on cool navy pinstripes. But it doesn't survive to 16px: rendered and pixel-inspected, the pointed shuttle silhouette collapses into a plain horizontal amber bar and the pinstripes vanish entirely, so all shuttle-specific identity is lost — you're left with an anonymous stripe on a dark square. Good dock presence, good idea, but the mark's meaning depends on a size it won't always be seen at.

Rendered and pixel-checked at 16px: unambiguous, high-contrast T, no competitor comes close — this is the only candidate that behaves like a real macOS app icon at every size (bold single glyph, generous padding, classic monogram convention). Craft is excellent (sheen, considered interlace joint at the crossbar). Weakest on brand-specificity though: the weave joint is a nice detail but reads to most viewers as 'a T logo,' not 'a loom' — it leans on the name more than the metaphor.

Elegant continuous-ribbon triquetra/trinity-knot, technically the most sophisticated bezier work of the four. Surprisingly legible at 16px (pixel-checked) — high thread/ground contrast lets three interlocking loops still read clearly, better than a naive read of 'six overlapping curves' would suggest. But conceptually it's the weakest fit: no warp/weft grid, no parallel strands, no shuttle — a single strand tied in a loop reads as generic Celtic-knot/rope-logo rather than 'loom,' and edges closer to the yarn/craft cliché the brief explicitly wants to avoid. Also the plate lacks the depth treatment (vignette/sheen) the other three have.

Rasterized check: the plain-weave grid keeps its bold color blocks down to 16px, but the over/under shadow rectangles at each crossing dissolve into grey moiré murk under magnification, so it reads as a textile swatch/plaid pattern rather than a single confident glyph. In the dock-row simulation it's colorful and holds contrast fine on both light and dark bars, but next to bolder single-shape icons it looks busier/more decorative — more 'fabric sample' than 'app.' Most literal and correct depiction of warp/weft plain weave of the four; precise, calm, unmistakably loom-related.

The lens/boat shuttle shape is a single warm, high-contrast silhouette that survives 16px cleanly — it's the kind of bold negative-space mark that reads at a glance. The vertical pinstripe field behind it gets a bit noisy/hazy at small sizes (visible in the 16px crop) but doesn't compete much since it's low-contrast against the shuttle's warm hue. Pops well on both simulated light and dark dock bars. Conceptually the most precise brand fit — literally a shuttle moving across threads, calm purposeful motion, zero yarn-cute risk. Construction is clean but simpler than A or C (fewer distinct techniques on display).

Best performer under actual rasterization: an isolated, bold, high-contrast T-letterform on a smooth gradient field with zero competing texture. In the dock-row simulation at both 32px and 64px it has the strongest 'pop' of the set — nothing else in the frame to dilute attention. The tradeoff is brand specificity: the woven-joint detail (the actual over/under crossing logic, technically the most sophisticated construction here) is precisely what disappears first at small sizes, so at 16px it reads as a well-made monogram 'T,' not distinctly a loom/weaving mark — a competent generic-app move dressed up with a clever detail most users will never resolve at icon size.

Weakest by a clear margin once actually rendered small: the trinity-knot interlace has too much internal dark negative space, so at 16px the 'ink' shrinks to a soft, low-contrast blob/smudge rather than a crisp mark — visibly the dimmest, least-resolved icon in the 32px dock-row simulation next to the other three. The six paths are simply stacked in z-order with no gap/under-crossing cut, so even at full size it reads as a tangled ribbon rather than a true precise weave — undercutting the 'craft' the brief asks for. Also risks generic Celtic-knot/wellness-logo association rather than warp-weft/shuttle specificity, and its soft closed-loop roundness edges toward the yarn-ball cute the brief explicitly rules out.
